reviewerOrPass: Worker B, same AI, separate source-first pass
method: After freezing and replaying the pair, returned to Annexes 4 and 5 and checked the component allocation and levels from the source. Independently checked each selected elective against the time-slot calendar and rechecked Article 4.2 progression before the thesis. Reconsidered the underlying UCR evidence for the new spatial planning, policy and public economics selections, the direct rows and the progression and purposes of all three schedules. This was a separate pass by the same AI.
findings: The 2026–27 Dutch-medium degree permits up to one-third of teaching in English. Annex 4 and the student major show eight compulsory first-year courses (60 EC), 30 EC across the four courses in one chosen track, 15 EC of major electives, three 5 EC final-year courses and a 15 EC thesis. The major totals 135 EC and profiling is 45 EC. The example takes Migration and Global Development, first in both the student major page and formal track list. The 2026–27 calendar rules out Storytelling for Open Cities (formerly Planning for Open Cities) in period 1 slot B and Transport Geography in period 2 slot A, because they share slots with the required theory and themes courses respectively. Planning Theory (period 1 C, GEO2-7011) and Geography, Representation and Media (period 2 C, GEO3-3405) are major electives in Annex 5 with distinct slots and no stated additional entry requirement in the corresponding minor lists. The year-two track and major electives account for 45 EC. Two remaining year-two slots and a first semester in year three can be filled with 15 and 30 EC of profiling respectively. At least 15 profiling EC must be at level 2 or above. The selected major has 45 EC at level 2 and 52.5 EC at level 3. The non-credit tutorial and study-career activities are listed separately by the calendar.

Article 4.2 requires participation in both first-block courses and passing one before Borders in Perspective. Track entry requires 45 earned EC, passing Globalization and Development, and participating in Spatial Data and Geographic Information and Socio-Spatial Research. Themes follows participation in Theory. The mixed-methods project follows participation in Themes and requires a pass in Spatial Data and Geographic Information. The practice atelier requires participation in Theory and Themes and a pass in one. All four track courses are taken in one academic year, with period and slot sequence 1B, 2A, 3D and 4D. Before Analysis, students pass the mixed-methods project. Before Research Design, they pass the first-year courses and complete the track. Before the thesis, they also pass Research Design and participate in Science and Society and Analysis. The final-year calendar puts the three 5 EC components in period 3 and the thesis in period 4. The student calendar is an illustration of current ordering and slots; it does not guarantee future offerings.

The broad response uses sustainability foundations and social-science methods to study urban and environmental change. Earth Observation develops spatial queries, mapping and remote sensing. The description-only Spatial Planning course directly adds applied GIS, disaster response, sustainable agriculture and environmental monitoring, with the gate already passed. Living with Water applies environmental risk and adaptation to delta settings. Earth System Science Tools supports interpretation of environmental change through proxies and models; it is not a planning course. Public economics, comparative constitutional law and property law give the urban governance plan a distinct emphasis on distribution, public services, rights and land-use institutions. Consumer Product Design primarily studies prototyping and production and was replaced by the more relevant Public Economics. The migration plan links forced migration and colonial histories with open-economy macroeconomics, human rights, global policy and cultural mobility. The description-only Public Policy Analysis uses a cross-scale globalization case and policy memos; its contribution is policy reasoning rather than specialist migration methods. Historical inquiry and qualitative methods supply research practice. The stakeholder project is offered only in the first term, so the two plans retain related applied work through distinct later courses. Three aligned rows cover concrete shared delta, GIS and empirical-research work. Eight previous alignments represented broader context or different methods and are separated. Utrecht retains advanced social-spatial research, a migration practice lab, planning theory and the required thesis. Sustainable cities and innovative regions remain documented candidate directions under the three-option cap; the broad option already uses tools for sustainability and spatial questions.
